Literal Sense

The Divine Command

Genesis 22 opens with one of the most dramatic scenes in all of Scripture: "After these things, God tempted Abraham, and said to him: Abraham, Abraham. And he answered: Here I am" (Gen 22:1). The Hebrew word nissah, translated as "tempted," means to test or prove, not to entice to evil. God tests Abraham not to learn something He does not know, but to reveal and perfect Abraham's faith.

St. John Chrysostom addresses this precise point in his Homilies on Hebrews:

"What then? Did not God know that the man was noble and approved? Why then did He tempt him? Not that He might Himself learn, but that He might show to others, and make his fortitude manifest to all."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Hebrews, 25

St. Augustine similarly explains the purpose of the divine test in his Questions on Genesis:

"The expression 'to know' should be understood as if it were said: 'to make you know', because the power of love itself is hidden from man, if God does not make it known through a test."

St. Augustine, Questions on Genesis

The Command to Sacrifice Isaac

The command itself is staggering in its specificity: "Take thy only begotten son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and go into the land of vision: and there thou shalt offer him for a holocaust upon one of the mountains which I will shew thee" (Gen 22:2). Each phrase intensifies the trial. Not merely "your son" but "your only begotten son" (yachid in Hebrew, monogenes in the Septuagint). Not merely Isaac but "Isaac, whom thou lovest." The threefold designation your son, your only son, whom you love mirrors the threefold divine characterization of Christ in the Gospels.

The land of Moriah (terra visionis, "land of vision") becomes the site of Solomon's Temple centuries later. According to 2 Chronicles 3:1: "Solomon began to build the house of the Lord in Jerusalem, on mount Moria, where the Lord had appeared to David his father, in the place which David had prepared in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite." The very mountain where Abraham stretched forth his hand to slay his son is where the Temple sacrifices would later be offered, and near where Christ would offer Himself on Calvary.

Abraham's Obedience

Abraham's response is immediate and without recorded protest: "So Abraham rising up in the night, saddled his ass: and took with him two young men, and Isaac his son: and when he had cut wood for the holocaust he went his way to the place which God had commanded him" (Gen 22:3). The text records no hesitation, no bargaining as in the case of Sodom, no questioning. Abraham simply obeys.

St. John Chrysostom marvels at the depth of this obedience:

"He heard the opposite of the promises from Him who had made them; and yet he was not disturbed, nor did he stagger, nor think he had been deceived. For they were in harmony; being opposed indeed according to human calculations, but in harmony when viewed by Faith."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Hebrews, 25

The Three-Day Journey

The journey to Moriah takes three days: "On the third day, lifting up his eyes, he saw the place afar off" (Gen 22:4). These three days are not merely geographical but theological. From the moment of the command, Isaac is as good as dead in Abraham's heart; the three days become a kind of death before the restoration. Origen, in his Homilies on Genesis, observes the mystical significance:

"The third day, however, is always applied to mysteries."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis, 8.4

Isaac Bears the Wood

At the foot of the mountain, Abraham takes the wood of the burnt offering and lays it upon Isaac: "And he took the wood for the holocaust, and laid it upon Isaac his son: and he himself carried in his hands fire and a sword" (Gen 22:6). Isaac, no longer a small child but likely a young man capable of carrying a substantial load of wood, ascends the mountain bearing the instrument of his own sacrifice.

The dialogue between father and son is exquisitely poignant: "Isaac said to his father: My father. And he answered: What wilt thou, son? Behold, saith he, fire and wood: where is the victim for the holocaust?" (Gen 22:7). Abraham's reply is both prophetic and faithful: "God will provide himself a victim for a holocaust, my son" (Gen 22:8).

St. John Chrysostom sees in Abraham's answer a genuine prophecy:

"In this he uttered a prophecy that God would provide Himself a burnt offering in His Son."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis

The Binding and the Intervention

Upon reaching the designated place, Abraham builds the altar, arranges the wood, binds Isaac, and lays him upon the altar. The Hebrew term for "binding" (akedah) gives this entire passage its Jewish name. Then the climactic moment: "He put forth his hand and took the sword, to sacrifice his son" (Gen 22:10).

At the last possible moment, the angel of the Lord calls from heaven: "Abraham, Abraham... Lay not thy hand upon the boy, neither do thou any thing to him: now I know that thou fearest God, and hast not spared thy only begotten son for my sake" (Gen 22:11-12). The phrase "now I know" does not indicate that God learned something new, as Augustine carefully explains:

"The phrase 'I know now that you fear God' means 'now I make you known' that is, God was revealing Abraham's faith rather than learning something new about him."

St. Augustine, Questions on Genesis

The Ram in the Thicket

Abraham then sees a ram caught in a thicket by its horns: "Abraham lifted up his eyes, and saw behind his back a ram amongst the briers sticking fast by the horns, which he took and offered for a holocaust instead of his son" (Gen 22:13). The ram is provided by God as a substitute, and Abraham names the place Jehovah-jireh, "The Lord will provide" or "The Lord will see."

The Divine Oath

The chapter concludes with God's oath confirming His covenant with Abraham: "By my own self have I sworn, saith the Lord: because thou hast done this thing, and hast not spared thy only begotten son for my sake: I will bless thee, and I will multiply thy seed as the stars of heaven, and as the sand that is by the sea shore" (Gen 22:16-17). This is the first time in Scripture that God swears by Himself, the supreme oath as the Epistle to the Hebrews explains: "For men swear by one greater than themselves... wherein God, meaning more abundantly to shew to the heirs of the promise the immutability of his counsel, interposed an oath" (Heb 6:16-17).
allegorical:
Allegorical Sense

Isaac as Type of Christ

No passage of the Old Testament has been more consistently and universally interpreted as a type of Christ than Genesis 22. The Binding of Isaac (the Akedah) is, in the words of the Church Fathers, a "sketch ahead of time in shadow" of the sacrifice of God's only begotten Son. Melito of Sardis, in his second-century Homily on the Pascha, explicitly names Isaac among the figures who prefigured Christ:

"This one is the passover of our salvation. This is the one who patiently endured many things in many people: This is the one who was murdered in Abel, and bound as a sacrifice in Isaac, and exiled in Jacob, and sold in Joseph, and exposed in Moses, and sacrificed in the lamb, and hunted down in David, and dishonored in the prophets."

Melito of Sardis, Peri Pascha (On the Passover), 69

Melito further instructs:

"If you desire to see the mystery of the Lord, pay close attention to Abel who likewise was put to death, to Isaac who likewise was bound hand and foot, to Joseph who likewise was sold, to Moses who likewise was exposed, to David who likewise was hunted down, to the prophets who likewise suffered because they were the Lord's anointed."

Melito of Sardis, Peri Pascha, 59

The Only Begotten Son

The divine characterization of Isaac as "your only begotten son... whom you love" (Gen 22:2) directly parallels the Father's declaration at Christ's baptism and transfiguration: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matt 3:17). The term monogenes (only begotten) used in the Septuagint is the same word St. John uses of Christ: "God so loved the world, as to give his only begotten Son" (John 3:16). As Abraham did not spare his only begotten son, so the Father did not spare His own Son but delivered Him up for us all (Rom 8:32).

St. Augustine, in his City of God, develops this parallel:

"Just as the Lord carried his cross, so Isaac himself carried to the place of sacrifice the wood on which he too was to be placed."

St. Augustine, City of God

Isaac Carries the Wood

The image of Isaac bearing the wood up the mountain is the most striking typological correspondence. Origen expounds this at length in his Homilies on Genesis:

"Isaac himself carries the wood for his own holocaust: this is a figure of Christ. For he bore the burden of the cross, and yet to carry the wood for the holocaust is really the duty of the priest. He is then both victim and priest."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis, 8

Tertullian and Irenaeus likewise stress this parallel: Isaac carries the wood that would be prepared for his death, just as Jesus carried His cross to Golgotha. The early Christian sarcophagi frequently depicted the sacrifice of Isaac balanced by scenes from Christ's Passion, visually expressing this typological connection.

The Third Day

The three-day journey to Moriah prefigures Christ's three days in the tomb. Isaac is given up to death in Abraham's heart on the first day; for three days Abraham walks in grief; on the third day Isaac is figuratively restored from the dead. The Epistle to the Hebrews makes this explicit: "By faith Abraham, when he was tried, offered Isaac... accounting that God is able to raise up even from the dead. Wherefrom also he received him in a similitude" (Heb 11:17, 19). The Greek en parabole ("in a similitude" or "figuratively speaking") indicates that Isaac's restoration was a parable of resurrection.

Origen observes the mystical significance of this timing:

"The third day, however, is always applied to mysteries."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis, 8.4

Mount Moriah and Calvary

The location is profoundly significant. Mount Moriah, where Isaac was bound, is identified with the Temple Mount in Jerusalem. Golgotha, where Christ was crucified, lies just outside the city walls, within the same ridge system. The typological connection was not lost on the Fathers. Abraham's prophetic word, "God will provide Himself a victim," finds its ultimate fulfillment not in the ram but in the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.

The Ram Caught in the Thicket

The ram provided by God as a substitute for Isaac carries its own Christological significance. Theodoret of Cyrus offers a distinctive interpretation:

"Isaac is a symbol of Christ's divinity and the ram is a symbol of His humanity."

Theodoret of Cyrus, Questions on Genesis, 74

The ram caught by its horns in the thorns (sabek) has been read as prefiguring Christ crowned with thorns. As the ram was entangled and could not free itself, so Christ willingly submitted to His Passion. Athanasius of Alexandria writes:

"And when he was tried, by faith he offered up Isaac, and sacrificed his only-begotten son he who had received the promises. And, in offering his son, he worshipped the Son of God. And, being restrained from sacrificing Isaac, he saw the Messiah in the ram, which was offered up instead as a sacrifice to God."

St. Athanasius of Alexandria

Origen explains the dual typology of Isaac and the ram:

"In this respect, the ram is the type, just as John said: 'Behold the lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world.' The Word, however, remained incorruptible. This is Christ according to the spirit, and Isaac is the type. Therefore, Christ himself is both victim and priest according to the spirit. For he offers the victim to the Father according to the flesh, and he is himself offered on the altar of the cross."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis, 8

Abraham as Type of the Father

If Isaac is a type of Christ the Son, then Abraham is a type of God the Father. Theodoret of Cyrus recognizes this:

"All these were shadows of the economy of our salvation. The Father offered his well-beloved Son for the world."

Theodoret of Cyrus

Irenaeus of Lyons expounds this parallel in Against Heresies:

"Abraham, according to his faith, followed the command of the Word of God, and with a ready mind delivered up, as a sacrifice to God, his only-begotten and beloved son, in order that God also might be pleased to offer up for all his seed His own beloved and only-begotten Son, as a sacrifice for our redemption."

St. Irenaeus of Lyons, Against Heresies, IV.5.4

The crucial difference, of course, is that Isaac was spared at the last moment, while Christ was not. The angel stayed Abraham's hand; no angel intervened at Calvary. God did what He prevented Abraham from doing He gave His only begotten Son to death for our salvation.

Isaac's Willing Submission

A remarkable feature of the narrative is Isaac's apparent willingness. Though old enough to carry the wood and certainly capable of resisting his aged father, Isaac submits to being bound and placed on the altar. Hippolytus of Rome reflects on this in his Commentary on the Song of Songs:

"The blessed Isaac became desirous of the anointing and he wished to sacrifice himself for the sake of the world."

St. Hippolytus of Rome, Commentary on the Song of Songs, 2:15

This willing submission prefigures Christ's own words: "No man taketh my life away from me: but I lay it down of myself, and I have power to lay it down: and I have power to take it up again" (John 10:18).

Jehovah-Jireh: The Lord Will Provide

Abraham's naming of the place, Jehovah-jireh ("The Lord will see" or "The Lord will provide"), becomes a permanent testimony to divine providence in salvation. The Fathers understood this as pointing forward to God's provision of Christ. Caesarius of Arles, in his sermon on this passage, writes:

"The government of Christ of which we read: 'And the government shall be upon his shoulders,' is none other than His cross. For this reason this lesson is read at Easter when the true Isaac, whose type the son of Abraham showed, is fastened to the gibbet of the cross for the human race."

Caesarius of Arles, Sermon 84
moral:
Moral Sense

The Obedience of Faith

Genesis 22 presents the supreme biblical example of the obedience that flows from faith. Abraham's response to the divine command, with no recorded hesitation or objection, establishes the pattern for all who would follow God. The New Testament explicitly holds up Abraham's obedience as exemplary:

"Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he offered Isaac his son upon the altar? Seest thou, that faith did co-work with his works; and by works faith was made perfect?" (James 2:21-22)

St. John Chrysostom, in his Homilies on Hebrews, explains the nature of Abraham's trial:

"With regard to Abraham, it was different. He was enjoined to do what was opposed to the promises; and yet not even so was he troubled, nor did he stagger, nor think he had been deceived. Great indeed was the faith of Abraham."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Hebrews, 25

The moral lesson is profound: true faith manifests itself in obedience, even when obedience seems to contradict God's own promises. Abraham had been promised that through Isaac his seed would be multiplied as the stars of heaven. Now God commands him to sacrifice Isaac. Faith trusts that God can reconcile what appears irreconcilable. Chrysostom elaborates:

"By the same faith by which he believed that God gave what was not, and raised up the dead, by the same was he persuaded that He would also raise him up after he had been slain in sacrifice."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Hebrews, 25

The Fear of God

The angel's declaration, "Now I know that thou fearest God" (Gen 22:12), reveals the purpose of the trial: to demonstrate and perfect the holy fear that is the beginning of wisdom. The "fear of God" here is not servile terror but filial reverence the disposition of a soul that loves God above all things and would rather lose everything than offend Him.

Abraham's fear of God was proved by his willingness to sacrifice what he loved most. The moral application is direct: we demonstrate our fear of God not merely by avoiding obvious sins but by our willingness to surrender even legitimate goods when God calls us to do so. Every Christian faces smaller "Moriahs" throughout life opportunities to prove that we love God more than His gifts.

The Surrender of What We Love

Isaac was not merely Abraham's son; he was the child of promise, the fulfillment of decades of longing, the vessel of all Abraham's hopes for the future. To sacrifice Isaac would mean, in human terms, the end of everything Abraham had waited for and believed in.

The moral lesson extends to all who follow God: we must be willing to surrender even our deepest desires, our most cherished hopes, and our most legitimate loves when God calls us to do so. This is the meaning of our Lord's words: "If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple" (Luke 14:26). The "hatred" Christ demands is not emotional animosity but a willingness to prefer God above all else.

Immediate Obedience

The text emphasizes the immediacy of Abraham's obedience: "Abraham rising up in the night, saddled his ass" (Gen 22:3). He did not delay until morning; he did not take time to deliberate further. Once God's will was clear, he acted immediately.

The moral implication is that delayed obedience is a form of disobedience. When God's will is known, the faithful soul responds at once. Procrastination in spiritual matters often indicates a divided heart, a desire to serve God on our own terms rather than His.

The Strength of the Elderly

We should not overlook that Abraham was well over one hundred years old when he undertook this journey and climbed Mount Moriah. Age had not diminished his faith or his capacity for obedience. The moral lesson for the elderly is that God may call them to their greatest trials and their finest hours in their last years. For the young, it is a reminder that faithfulness sustained over a lifetime prepares the soul for whatever God may ask.

Isaac's Obedience

Isaac's willing submission to his father offers a complementary moral lesson. Though capable of resistance, Isaac allowed himself to be bound and placed on the altar. This teaches the virtue of filial obedience the trust that children owe to parents who lead them in the way of God. More broadly, it models submission to divine providence even when that providence leads through suffering.

Trust in Divine Providence

Abraham's answer to Isaac's question, "God will provide himself a victim for a holocaust" (Gen 22:8), expresses the heart of trust in divine providence. Abraham did not know how God would fulfill His promise, but he trusted that God would provide. This is the essence of Christian hope: not knowledge of how God will act, but confidence that He will act for our good.

The naming of the place, Jehovah-jireh ("The Lord will provide"), becomes a permanent memorial to this truth. In every trial, the Christian can look to Moriah and remember that the God who provided for Abraham will provide for all who trust in Him.

Faith and Reason

Chrysostom notes that Abraham's faith operated above human calculation:

"He was not disturbed, but did them as if they had been in harmony. For they were in harmony; being opposed indeed according to human calculations, but in harmony when viewed by Faith."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Hebrews, 25

The moral lesson is that faith does not abandon reason but transcends it. When God's commands seem to conflict with His promises or with human logic, faith trusts that God sees what we cannot see and that His ways are higher than our ways. This does not mean blind credulity but rather the humble recognition that the infinite God may have purposes beyond our finite comprehension.

The Reward of Faithfulness

The chapter concludes with God's oath confirming and expanding His promises to Abraham. Having proved faithful in the supreme test, Abraham receives the supreme blessing. The moral lesson is that God rewards those who trust Him. What we surrender to God is never truly lost; what we cling to apart from God can never truly satisfy. Abraham received Isaac back as one risen from the dead, and he received as well the eternal blessing that flows through his seed to all nations.
anagogical:
Anagogical Sense

The Sacrifice of Christ and Eternal Redemption

The anagogical sense of Genesis 22 points beyond the historical event to its ultimate fulfillment in Christ's eternal sacrifice and the heavenly realities thereby secured. What was shadowed on Mount Moriah was accomplished on Calvary, and what was accomplished on Calvary echoes through eternity in the heavenly sanctuary.

The Epistle to the Hebrews makes explicit the eschatological dimension of Abraham's faith. With the coming of Christ, the account in Genesis 22 assumes a more profound meaning: the faith of Abraham becomes a faith in the power of God to raise from the dead, and the oath made to Abraham finds its fulfillment in the oath made by God to Jesus at the moment of His resurrection, so that His earthly priesthood becomes a heavenly priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek (cf. Heb 6:13-20; 7:20-22).

Christ's sacrifice is not merely a historical event but an eternal reality. "Christ is not entered into the holies made with hands, the patterns of the true: but into heaven itself, that he may appear now in the presence of God for us" (Heb 9:24). The Lamb who was slain on Calvary stands forever in heaven as the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world (Rev 13:8).

The Resurrection and the Third Day

The three-day journey to Moriah, culminating in Isaac's figurative restoration from death, points to the resurrection of Christ on the third day. This is not merely typological but eschatological: the resurrection of Christ is the firstfruits of the general resurrection, the guarantee that all who belong to Christ will be raised at His coming.

The Apostle Paul teaches: "Now Christ is risen from the dead, the firstfruits of them that sleep. For by a man came death, and by a man the resurrection of the dead. And as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive" (1 Cor 15:20-22). The "third day" of Genesis 22 thus looks forward not only to Easter Sunday but to the last day when all the dead shall rise.

The Heavenly Priesthood

Origen's observation that Isaac was "both victim and priest" finds its fulfillment in Christ's eternal priesthood. On Calvary, Christ offered Himself once for all; in heaven, He continues His priestly ministry forever:

"Christ himself is both victim and priest according to the spirit. For he offers the victim to the Father according to the flesh, and he is himself offered on the altar of the cross."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis, 8

This eternal priesthood is the foundation of Christian hope. "He is able also to save for ever them that come to God by him; always living to make intercession for us" (Heb 7:25). What Abraham began when he interceded for Sodom (Gen 18), and what was typified when Isaac was spared through divine intervention, finds its eternal reality in Christ's unceasing intercession before the Father.

The Oath of God and the Certainty of Salvation

God's oath to Abraham, "By my own self have I sworn" (Gen 22:16), establishes the unshakeable foundation of Christian hope. The Epistle to the Hebrews explicitly connects this oath to the certainty of our salvation:

"Wherein God, meaning more abundantly to shew to the heirs of the promise the immutability of his counsel, interposed an oath: That by two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have the strongest comfort, who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us. Which we have as an anchor of the soul, sure and firm" (Heb 6:17-19).

The anagogical meaning is that our eternal salvation rests not on our own faithfulness but on God's sworn promise. The God who swore to Abraham has sworn to all who believe in Christ. This oath cannot fail; this promise cannot be broken. The "anchor of the soul" is fixed in heaven itself, where Christ has entered as our forerunner.

The Heavenly Jerusalem

Mount Moriah, where Isaac was bound and the Temple later built, points to the heavenly Jerusalem. The earthly Jerusalem was a copy and shadow of the heavenly city (Heb 8:5). The sacrifices offered there prefigured the one sacrifice of Christ. Now, through Christ, believers approach not the earthly mountain but the heavenly:

"You are come to mount Sion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the company of many thousands of angels, and to the church of the firstborn, who are written in the heavens, and to God the judge of all, and to the spirits of the just made perfect, and to Jesus the mediator of the new testament, and to the sprinkling of blood which speaketh better than that of Abel" (Heb 12:22-24).

The blood of Christ "speaks better than Abel" speaks better too than the ram on Moriah. That blood has opened heaven itself; through it we have access to the throne of grace; by it we shall enter the eternal inheritance.

The Multiplication of the Seed

God's promise to multiply Abraham's seed "as the stars of heaven, and as the sand that is by the sea shore" (Gen 22:17) looks beyond earthly Israel to the innumerable company of the redeemed in heaven. Alcuin of York interpreted these images eschatologically:

"By the stars of heaven are understood the fewer, stronger and more brilliant people, and by the sand of the sea shore the great multitude of the weak and carnal."

Alcuin of York

St. John's vision in Revelation depicts the fulfillment: "After this I saw a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne, and in sight of the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands" (Rev 7:9). These are the true seed of Abraham, those who share his faith and inherit his blessing through Christ.

The Blessing of All Nations

The promise that "in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed" (Gen 22:18) finds its eschatological fulfillment in the ingathering of the Gentiles and the final salvation of all who believe. Christ is the seed of Abraham par excellence, and through Him the blessing flows to every nation.

The anagogical completion awaits the end of history, when "at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth: and that every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father" (Phil 2:10-11). What began with Abraham's obedience on Moriah culminates in the universal worship of Christ in eternity.

The Final Victory Over Death

The Binding of Isaac, read anagogically, proclaims the ultimate defeat of death. Isaac was figuratively raised from the dead; Christ was literally raised; and at the last day, all who are in Christ shall be raised to eternal life. "Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy victory? O death, where is thy sting?" (1 Cor 15:54-55).

The God who provided a ram for Abraham, who raised Christ from the dead, will raise all His children to everlasting life. The "land of vision" (Moriah) becomes a window into the ultimate vision: the beatific vision of God Himself, where the faithful shall see Him face to face and know as they are known.

The Joy of the Promise Fulfilled

The name Isaac means "laughter." Sarah laughed in doubt; she later laughed in joy at his birth. Abraham rejoiced to see Christ's day and was glad (John 8:56). The anagogical meaning is that all the sorrows of faith will be transformed into the joy of vision. The trials of Moriah give way to the joys of heaven. "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes: and death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor sorrow shall be any more, for the former things are passed away" (Rev 21:4).

What Abraham believed in hope, we await in hope. What Isaac experienced in type, we shall experience in reality. The sacrifice has been offered; the resurrection has begun; the inheritance is secured. We await only the final manifestation, when faith shall become sight and hope shall become possession, and all the shadows of Moriah shall give way to the eternal light of the Lamb.
